_comment: The twin vector table for the net fence (card 201). Card 199's fence lives in
Java and judges the address a tool was HANDED. The browser's own request hook
lives in the Electron shell, in TypeScript, and judges every redirect hop and
every subresource — the hole browse_page documents in its own javadoc and
cannot close. Two languages, one policy, and nothing but a shared habit to
keep them equal.
So they are not kept equal by habit. Both sides read THIS file:
Java  spectro-core .../browser/FenceVectorTwinTest.java
TS    spectro-desktop/src/browserFence.test.ts
A rule added on one side and forgotten on the other turns one of them red.
The table has two halves because the fence has two questions. `vectors` are
address literals and loopback NAMES, which both sides decide without asking
a resolver. `names` are host names with the answer WRITTEN DOWN, so both
sides can be driven by the same DNS answer without a network: Java through
NetFence.Resolver, the hook through its HostLookup seam.
The names half was added on 2026-08-13 after a review measured what its
absence cost. The hook used to skip DNS entirely, and the comment here said
so as if it were a documented split; it was a hole. With allowLocalhost OFF,
a 302 to a public name that resolves to 127.0.0.1 loaded, titled itself
PWNED, and produced zero refusals. Java refused the same address at the
entry, so the table recorded no disagreement — which is exactly the shape a
vector table has to catch and did not. Both halves now resolve.
One row of that review stands: the register carried only divergences where
JAVA is looser and the hook catches it. That is the comfortable direction.
The two vectors below marked (was a hook hole) are the other direction,
measured and now closed, and they are ordinary vectors precisely because
the two sides agree again.
What is deliberately NOT here: IPv4-compatible (`::192.168.1.1`) and NAT64
(`64:ff9b::192.168.1.1`) spellings. Both sides read them as ordinary IPv6
addresses and allow them, and they agree because they are right: neither
reaches the embedded v4 address without translation infrastructure in the
path. Measured on this JDK and this Chromium on 2026-08-13.
The addresses are stand-ins from NoOperatorAddressesInTheRepoTest's curated
list. This repository is public; a real host never goes in a test.
_names_comment: Host NAMES, with the DNS answer stated so both halves can be driven by the
same answer offline. `localtest.example` stands in for the public name that
resolves to loopback — the reviewer used the real one live; a suite that
needs the network is a suite that is red on a train.
The rule is the same on both sides and is the one thing worth stating: EVERY
answer is judged, and ONE private answer refuses the request. A name with a
public A record and a private AAAA record is refused.
_divergences_comment: Where the two halves honestly answer differently, measured 2026-08-13 on this
JDK 21 and Node 25 / Chromium 150. Listed rather than dropped, and both sides
assert their own column, so a divergence cannot change in silence.
The cause is one thing: WHO parses the host. Java hands the string to
InetAddress, which is exactly what the connector will dial, so the entry check
judges the address the JVM would reach. The hook is inside Chromium and the
WHATWG URL parser has already normalised the host, so it judges the address
the BROWSER will reach. The two parsers disagree about old IPv4 spellings.
The second row is the interesting one and is the argument for having the hook
at all: Java reads 0177.0.0.1 as 177.0.0.1 — a public address — and the entry
check therefore allows it, while Chromium reads the same string as octal
loopback and dials 127.0.0.1. Only the in-hook fence sees what was actually
dialled, and it refuses. Neither half is wrong about its own process; the
browser's own hook is the one that decides where the browser goes.

divergences.why: InetAddress refuses the hex spelling; the WHATWG parser reads it as 127.0.0.1. Both refuse.
InetAddress reads this as 177.0.0.1 (public) and allows it; Chromium reads octal loopback and the hook refuses. The hook is the half that governs where the browser goes.
